items.stem: State what is meant by the term "water quality".
items.answer: The chemical, physical and biological characteristics of water that determine its suitability for drinking, farming, industry and ecosystems
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the chemical, physical and biological characteristics of water that determine its suitability for drinking, farming, industry and ecosystems. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Alessia writes: "Water scarcity is only about quantity." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Quality is equally important: polluted water reduces usable supply and harms health.
items.markingKey: Quality is equally important: polluted water reduces usable supply and harms health. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why poor water quality reduces water availability.
items.answer: Polluted water cannot be used for drinking or irrigation without costly treatment, so the effective supply is smaller - e.g. the polluted Yamuna in Delhi or the Ganges.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Polluted water cannot be used for drinking or irrigation without costly treatment, so the effective supply is smaller - e.g. the polluted Yamuna in Delhi or the Ganges. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: The groundwater level below the surface at a borehole in the Central Valley was 27.5 m in 1990 and 40.0 m in 2010. Calculate the percentage change over the period.
items.markingKey: M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100 = (40.0 − 27.5) ÷ 27.5 × 100; A1 +45.5% (sign or "increase/decrease" required).

items.stem: Using a named example, outline two consequences of poor water quality.
items.answer: e.g. Lake Erie 2014: a toxic algal bloom (microcystin) left about 400,000 people in Toledo without drinking water for three days; fisheries and tourism were affected.
items.markingKey: e.g. Lake Erie 2014: a toxic algal bloom (microcystin) left about 400,000 people in Toledo without drinking water for three days; fisheries and tourism were affected.

items.stem: Outline one argument for and one argument against the view that water quality is now a greater threat to water security than water quantity.
items.answer: Both threaten security; quality issues are more widespread, while quantity crises are more acute.
items.markingKey: For: pollution reduces usable supply (Yamuna, Lake Erie). Against: droughts and over-abstraction cause acute shortages (Cape Town). [4]: 1 mark for a valid argument for, 1 for its development; 1 mark for a valid argument against, 1 for its development; generic points without geographical context are capped at 2.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "physical water scarcity"?
options: The coordinated management of land, water and related resources across a whole drainage basin, involving all stakeholders, to maximise economic and social welfare sustainably
A situation where water resources are insufficient to meet all demands, typically in arid regions, with over 75% of river flows withdrawn
The chemical, physical and biological characteristics of water that determine its suitability for drinking, farming, industry and ecosystems
Tension between riparian states when upstream use (dams, abstraction, pollution) affects downstream users
items.answer: A situation where water resources are insufficient to meet all demands, typically in arid regions, with over 75% of river flows withdrawn
items.markingKey: B. "physical water scarcity" is a situation where water resources are insufficient to meet all demands, typically in arid regions, with over 75% of river flows withdrawn.

items.stem: Explain how eutrophication affects freshwater ecosystems.
items.answer: Nutrient enrichment causes algal blooms that block light; when algae die, bacterial decomposition uses up dissolved oxygen, killing fish and creating dead zones; some algae produce toxins.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Nutrient enrichment causes algal blooms that block light; when algae die, bacterial decomposition uses up dissolved oxygen, killing fish and creating dead zones; some algae produce toxins. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

If the population grows to 14.5 million with no change in supply, what would the new figure be?

items.stem: Examine the view that economic water scarcity is a more serious global problem than physical water scarcity.
items.answer: Economic scarcity affects more people and is more solvable, so it is the more serious immediate problem.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - for: affects far more people (sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia); causes disease and lost education. Against / limitations: physical scarcity is harder to solve and worsening with climate change; affects food production in major breadbaskets. A supported conclusion might be: Economic scarcity affects more people and is more solvable, so it is the more serious immediate problem. items.stem: Mateo writes: "Dams always prevent flooding downstream." Explain why this is inaccurate.

items.answer: Upstream states control the headwaters and can build dams or abstract water; downstream states depend on flows passing through other countries and are vulnerable to upstream decisions.

items.stem: Outline one argument for and one argument against the view that integrated drainage basin management is the most effective way to manage water resources.
items.answer: IDBM is the best framework in principle, though effectiveness depends on governance and political will.
items.markingKey: For: whole-basin approach balances uses and ecosystems (Murray-Darling). Against: difficult across borders and sectors; requires data and strong institutions. [4]: 1 mark for a valid argument for, 1 for its development; 1 mark for a valid argument against, 1 for its development; generic points without geographical context are capped at 2.

items.stem: "Water quality is now a greater threat to water security than water quantity." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Both threaten security; quality issues are more widespread, while quantity crises are more acute.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - arguments supporting the statement: pollution reduces usable supply (Yamuna, Lake Erie); arsenic, nitrates and microplastics affect huge populations. Arguments challenging it: droughts and over-abstraction cause acute shortages (Cape Town); climate change reduces quantity in many regions. Evaluation should weigh places, scales, perspectives and time. Judgement: Both threaten security; quality issues are more widespread, while quantity crises are more acute. items.stem: "Large dams are a sustainable way to manage water resources." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Dams can contribute to sustainability only if well sited and managed; small-scale and integrated approaches are often more sustainable.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - arguments supporting the statement: long life, renewable energy, storage; adaptation to variable rainfall. Arguments challenging it: sedimentation reduces lifespan; reservoir emissions; social costs and loss of river ecosystems. Evaluation should weigh places, scales, perspectives and time. Judgement: Dams can contribute to sustainability only if well sited and managed; small-scale and integrated approaches are often more sustainable. items.stem:
Study the infographic / visual stimulus described below.

Table: Aral Sea area (km²) - 1960: 68,000; 1989: 40,000; 2007: 17,400; 2014: about 7,000 (excluding seasonal areas).

(a) Calculate the percentage reduction between 1960 and 2014. [4]
(b) Using the resource and your own knowledge, describe the rate of change shown. [6]
items.answer: (a) (7,000 − 68,000)/68,000 × 100 = -89.7% (b) Decline throughout, from about 970 km² a year (1960-89) to about 1,250 km² a year (1989-2007) and then about 1,490 km² a year (2007-14).
items.markingKey: (a) (7,000 − 68,000)/68,000 × 100 = -89.7% (b) Decline throughout, from about 970 km² a year (1960-89) to about 1,250 km² a year (1989-2007) and then about 1,490 km² a year (2007-14). Credit relevant own knowledge and named examples in (b). Infographic markscheme [10]: part (a) [4] - award 1 mark per valid point taken from the resource (data must be quoted with units for full marks); part (b) [6] - up to 2 marks for each developed explanation linking the resource to own knowledge; reward named examples; maximum 3 marks if the resource is not used.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "upstream-downstream conflict".
items.answer: Tension between riparian states when upstream use (dams, abstraction, pollution) affects downstream users
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: tension between riparian states when upstream use (dams, abstraction, pollution) affects downstream users. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The chemical, physical and biological characteristics of water that determine its suitability for drinking, farming, industry and ecosystems"?
items.answer: water quality
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of water quality.

items.stem: Define the term "hydroelectric power (HEP)".
items.answer: Electricity generated by water flowing through turbines, usually from a reservoir behind a dam
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: electricity generated by water flowing through turbines, usually from a reservoir behind a dam. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Tariq writes: "The Aral Sea disaster was caused by climate change." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: It was caused mainly by Soviet diversion of rivers for cotton irrigation from the 1960s.
items.markingKey: It was caused mainly by Soviet diversion of rivers for cotton irrigation from the 1960s. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam has caused tension in the Nile basin.
items.answer: Ethiopia sees it as essential for electricity and development; Egypt, which depends on the Nile for about 97% of its water, fears reduced flows during filling and droughts; no binding agreement on filling and operation was reached.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Ethiopia sees it as essential for electricity and development; Egypt, which depends on the Nile for about 97% of its water, fears reduced flows during filling and droughts; no binding agreement on filling and operation was reached. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Countries with high rainfall cannot suffer from water scarcity." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: They can suffer economic scarcity or pollution-related scarcity, e.g. Bangladesh's arsenic-contaminated groundwater.
items.markingKey: They can suffer economic scarcity or pollution-related scarcity, e.g. Bangladesh's arsenic-contaminated groundwater. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Mateo writes: "The benefits of dams are shared equally." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Benefits often go to urban consumers and commercial farmers while displaced rural and indigenous people bear the costs.
items.markingKey: Benefits often go to urban consumers and commercial farmers while displaced rural and indigenous people bear the costs. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why wetlands have been lost worldwide.
items.answer: Drainage for agriculture, urban expansion, dams and abstraction reducing inflows, pollution and peat extraction; about 35% of wetlands have been lost since 1970.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Drainage for agriculture, urban expansion, dams and abstraction reducing inflows, pollution and peat extraction; about 35% of wetlands have been lost since 1970. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Wars over water between states are common." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Interstate "water wars" are rare; most transboundary water relations involve cooperation or diplomatic tension, though water adds to wider conflicts.
items.markingKey: Interstate "water wars" are rare; most transboundary water relations involve cooperation or diplomatic tension, though water adds to wider conflicts. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe arsenic in Bangladesh's groundwater and explain what it reveals about the role of water quality in water security.
items.answer: Millions of shallow tube wells drilled from the 1970s exposed tens of millions of people to arsenic levels above WHO guidelines. Water that was abundant became unsafe, creating a public health crisis.
items.markingKey: Context (Millions of shallow tube wells drilled from the 1970s exposed tens of millions of people to arsenic levels above WHO guidelines.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Water that was abundant became unsafe, creating a public health crisis. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the role of water quality in water security.

items.stem: Between 1990 and 2005 the volume of water stored in a reservoir in South Africa changed from 2,516 to 2,521 million m³. Calculate the percentage change over the period.
items.markingKey: M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100 = (2,521 − 2,516) ÷ 2,516 × 100; A1 +0.2% (sign or "increase/decrease" required).

items.stem: Using a named example, outline two consequences of the loss of a wetland or inland water body.
items.answer: e.g. the Aral Sea: the fishing industry at Muynak and Aralsk collapsed (about 40,000 jobs lost); exposed salty, pesticide-laden seabed caused dust storms and respiratory disease.
items.markingKey: e.g. the Aral Sea: the fishing industry at Muynak and Aralsk collapsed (about 40,000 jobs lost); exposed salty, pesticide-laden seabed caused dust storms and respiratory disease.

items.stem: India has total renewable water resources of about 1911 km³ per year and a population of about 1428.6 million. Calculate the renewable water available per person (m³ per year) and classify it using the Falkenmark indicator (1,700 / 1,000 / 500 m³). If the population grows to 1857.2 million with no change in supply, what would the new figure be?
items.answer: 1,338 m³/person/yr (water stress); future 1,029 m³/person/yr
items.markingKey: M1 km³ × 10⁹ ÷ population; A1 1,338 m³; R1 water stress; A1 1,029 m³.

items.stem: Suggest two strategies that could reduce economic water scarcity in rural Africa.
items.answer: Low-cost boreholes with hand pumps maintained by communities; rainwater harvesting tanks; community water committees and NGO-funded infrastructure (e.g. WaterAid).
items.markingKey: Low-cost boreholes with hand pumps maintained by communities; rainwater harvesting tanks; community water committees and NGO-funded infrastructure (e.g. WaterAid).

items.stem:
Study the infographic / visual stimulus described below.

Map description: the Mekong flows about 4,900 km from the Tibetan Plateau through China (Lancang), Myanmar, Laos, Thailand, Cambodia and Vietnam; China has built 11 large dams on the main stem; the Tonlé Sap lake in Cambodia reverses flow seasonally.

(a) Identify the upstream and downstream states. [4]
(b) Using the resource and your own knowledge, suggest one impact of upstream dams on the Tonlé Sap. [6]
items.answer: (a) Upstream: China (and Myanmar); downstream: Laos, Thailand, Cambodia and Vietnam (delta). (b) Lower wet-season flows reduce the reverse flow that fills the lake, cutting fish stocks that provide much of Cambodia's protein.
items.markingKey: (a) Upstream: China (and Myanmar); downstream: Laos, Thailand, Cambodia and Vietnam (delta). (b) Lower wet-season flows reduce the reverse flow that fills the lake, cutting fish stocks that provide much of Cambodia's protein. Credit relevant own knowledge and named examples in (b).
